stops.name: Geneva: La Fête de Juin, a city becomes a chorus
stops.campa: Over eight performances at the Théâtre du Centenaire, more than a thousand performers and a full symphony orchestra enact the four centuries of Geneva's road into the Swiss Confederation before packed grandstands on the shore of the lake. It is the summit of his civic-pageant art, larger than the Poème alpestre and the Festival vaudois combined, and it is an immense and undisputed triumph: the last entirely happy season, the canon will note, before Europe's own rhythm breaks beyond anyone's power to compose it.

stops.name: Geneva, the war breaks over the summer's triumph
stops.campa: Within weeks of the Fête de Juin's last curtain, the Archduke's assassination at Sarajevo detonates the general war, and Germany's armies cross into Belgium and France. Jaques-Dalcroze and Harald Dohrn, Wolf's brother, try for a time by letter to imagine how the Hellerau school might be restored once the fighting stops; neither man yet grasps that it will not stop for four years, and that the man who built the theatre for him is barely six months in his grave. Geneva, neutral and watching, becomes for the second time in a year his only fixed ground.

stops.name: Geneva, news of the burning of Reims
stops.campa: On 19 September German shells set the roof of Reims Cathedral alight: the coronation church of Clovis and of Charles VII, the stone the whole French-speaking world reads as the nation's own crown. Geneva's papers carry the news within days, and French-speaking Switzerland's writers and artists move to protest: Jaques-Dalcroze, who has built his life's second half on German soil and among German patrons, adds his signature to the lists the Tribune de Genève will publish through the autumn, alongside the painter Ferdinand Hodler and dozens of others who had, until this month, called Germany a second home.

stops.name: Geneva: barred from Germany, Hellerau falls silent
stops.campa: The signature on the Reims protest is remembered in Germany, and the man who ran Hellerau's school for four years is quietly barred from re-entering the country that built it for him. The Bildungsanstalt, already bereft of Dohrn's money and now of its own director, cannot survive the war and folds within the year. Jaques-Dalcroze will never set foot in Hellerau again. What Reims cost the stone of a cathedral, it costs him a garden-city and a theatre; he does not recant the signature, and Geneva, once more, absorbs what Germany has let fall.

stops.name: Geneva, the Institut opens at the Terrassière
stops.campa: A subscription committee of Geneva citizens, determined not to lose the creator of rhythmics a second time, raises the funds for a new Institut Jaques-Dalcroze, which opens its doors in the former Salle de la Source on the Rue de la Terrassière. What Hellerau built in brick and light-stage, Geneva rebuilds in rented rooms and civic will; the method that a German garden-city once housed so lavishly returns, chastened by the war but intact, to the city of his marriage, his son, and his first Conservatoire post.

stops.name: Geneva: Les Premiers Souvenirs, the Institut's own pageant
stops.campa: With the war still grinding on beyond the neutral border, the young Institut mounts its own inaugural spectacle, Les premiers souvenirs, text by Jacques Chenevière set to Jaques-Dalcroze's music: a modest civic pageant beside the Fête de Juin's thousand performers, but proof that the Terrassière school is no mere refugee camp for a broken German enterprise. It has its own stage, its own rites, its own graduating dancers. The method has found, at last, a home that cannot be closed by a foreign war office.

stops.name: Geneva, La Fête de la Jeunesse et de la Joie
stops.campa: Nine years after the Fête de Juin, he composes a new civic pageant, La Fête de la Jeunesse et de la Joie, the festival of youth and joy, with Nina Faliero-Dalcroze again among the principal performers. Where the 1914 pageant carried the freight of a nation's history, this one is offered as a plain gift to a Europe still nursing its wounds: youth and gladness staged as antidotes, deliberately, to the four years just past. The pattern of his life is now fixed: Geneva calls him for its great civic occasions as automatically as it once doubted his bare-footed classroom.

stops.name: Geneva and Paris: honorary citizen, a Paris branch
stops.campa: On 21 November 1925 the Republic and Canton of Geneva names him an honorary citizen: the sixty-year-old Vienna-born son of a clock-salesman formally adopted, in full civic ceremony, by the city that took his family in fifty years before. The same year sees a Paris branch of the Institut established, carrying the Terrassière's teaching into France proper; rhythmics, once a scandal to one Conservatoire, is now exported by two nations at once, taught by disciples who scatter from Geneva to London, Stockholm, Chicago, wherever a school will have them.

stops.name: Geneva, the First International Congress on Rhythm
stops.campa: The Institut convenes the first International Congress on Rhythm, drawing teachers, physicians and educators from across Europe to debate a discipline that, fourteen years after Hellerau, has outgrown any single school's authority over it. He presides as an elder statesman of a movement he began virtually alone in a Geneva harmony class, watching younger disciples, some trained under his own hand, some at one remove through Laban's and Wigman's rival schools of Ausdruckstanz, argue over a doctrine of the body that has by now split into several irreconcilable churches.

stops.name: Geneva, Officer of the Légion d'honneur
stops.campa: France, whose Opéra-Comique staged his youthful operas and whose Reims cathedral he protested for, names him Officer of the Légion d'honneur, adding a French decoration to the Swiss honorary citizenship of four years before. The double honor closes, formally, the wound the Reims protest opened with Germany: the republic he defended in September 1914 now decorates the man who signed against its enemy's guns. He is sixty-four, and the Institut he founded amid the ashes of Hellerau has by now trained a generation that will carry rhythmics through a second war he cannot yet foresee.

stops.name: Geneva: a second war, a neutral shore
stops.campa: France falls and the Institut's Paris branch is cut off; Geneva, neutral again as it was in 1914, becomes once more his only unbroken ground. At seventy-five he no longer teaches daily, but the Terrassière school he built from a war's wreckage keeps its doors open through blackout and ration, training children and refugees alike in a discipline that asks nothing more of a body than that it learn to feel its own time. He publishes his memoir, Souvenirs, notes et critiques, that same wartime season, setting down at last, from Vienna to Algiers to Hellerau, the whole rhythm of a life spent teaching rhythm.

stops.name: Geneva, the laurels of old age
stops.campa: In the years after the second war's end the honors come one after another, as if the world wished to settle its account before it was too late: an honorary doctorate from the University of Lausanne in 1945, another from Clermont-Ferrand in 1948, and from his own city of Geneva that same year, the University conferring on its eighty-three-year-old citizen the degree it never thought to offer the young harmony teacher whose bare-footed classes it once found scandalous. He accepts each with the same plain courtesy he has shown every pupil since 1892.
